Man, 64 years old, no significant medical history, presenting with a left colon tumor revealed by subocclusive syndrome.  Thoraco-abdominal CT scan shows a 6 cm colonic mass and two liver metastases in segments II and V measuring 2.2 and 3 cm. CEA: 120 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, MSS. No extra-hepatic disease.
MDT Discussion: Metastases considered primarily resectable, symptomatic colonic lesion is the priority.
Model_Alone:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Resectable.  
- Rationale:  
  • Two hepatic metastases (2.2 cm in segment II, 3 cm in segment V) are solitary, ≤5 cm each, and located in segments that allow parenchymal‑sparing resections with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant.  
  • No radiologic evidence of extra‑hepatic disease.  
  • RAS wild‑type and MSS status do not affect surgical resectability.  
  • Patient has no significant comorbidities, suggesting sufficient physiologic reserve for major abdominal surgery.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Urgent left‑sided colon resection (segmental colectomy or left hemicolectomy) to relieve obstruction and obtain oncologic control of the primary tumor.  
   – Rationale: Symptomatic primary lesion is the immediate priority; resection also provides pathological staging and eliminates a source of future complications.  

B. After postoperative recovery (typically 2–4 weeks), perform staged liver‑directed surgery: anatomic or non‑anatomic segmentectomy of segment II and segment V (or combined limited hepatectomy) preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.  
   – Rationale: Staged approach allows assessment of postoperative hepatic function and ensures safe margin attainment; lesions are amenable to curative‑intent resection with clear margins (R0).  

C. Adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX ± cetuximab given RAS wild‑type) initiated within 6–8 weeks after liver surgery.  
   – Rationale: High pre‑operative CEA (120 ng/mL) suggests aggressive biology; adjuvant therapy reduces recurrence risk.  

D. Surveillance protocol: CEA every 3 months for 2 years, contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen every 6 months, colonoscopy at 1 year.  
   – Rationale: Early detection of recurrence or new metastases improves long‑term outcomes.  

Step 3 – Missing information  
- Detailed performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky).  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin) and volumetric assessment of future liver remnant.  
- Presence of steatosis, fibrosis, or portal hypertension that could affect hepatic tolerance.  
- Exact relationship of the liver lesions to major vascular structures (portal/hepatic veins) to confirm feasibility of parenchymal‑sparing resection.  
- Patient’s preferences regarding simultaneous versus staged procedures.  
- Comprehensive comorbidity profile (cardiovascular, pulmonary, renal) and anesthetic risk assessment.  
- Pre‑operative nutritional status and serum albumin.  

Without these data, the plan assumes adequate hepatic reserve and operative fitness.

  • Two liver metastases (2.2 cm in segment II and 3 cm in segment V) are limited in number and size, allowing an R0 resection with preservation of ≥2 contiguous liver segments.  
  • Expected future liver remnant after left‑lateral sectionectomy (segments II‑III) plus a segment V resection would exceed the 30 % functional liver volume threshold for a normal liver.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on staging CT.  
  • Primary left‑colon tumor is symptomatic and amenable to curative resection (left hemicolectomy).  
  • Patient has no reported comorbidities that would preclude major abdominal surgery.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Pre‑operative work‑up  
   - Obtain high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to confirm lesion number, size, and relationship to vascular structures.  
   - Perform colonoscopy with biopsy to stage the primary (T/N status) and assess for obstruction.  
   - Calculate volumetric FLR; portal vein embolization is not anticipated.  
   - Optimize nutrition, assess cardiopulmonary fitness (ASA, ECOG).  

B. Surgical phase (simultaneous resection)  
   - Perform an oncologic left hemicolectomy with primary tumor removal and adequate lymphadenectomy.  
   - Conduct liver resection: left‑lateral sectionectomy (segments II‑III) plus anatomical segment V resection (or wedge) to achieve R0 margins (>1 mm).  
   - Rationale: the liver component is minor; simultaneous surgery avoids a second laparotomy, shortens overall treatment time, and is safe when the colorectal resection is not extensive.  

C. Post‑operative systemic therapy  
   - Initiate adjuvant chemotherapy within 6–8 weeks (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody given RAS‑wild‑type status).  
   - Rationale: synchronous disease, elevated pre‑operative CEA, and high‑risk primary tumor warrant systemic treatment to eradicate micrometastatic disease and improve disease‑free survival.  

D. Surveillance  
   - Monitor CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
   - Cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) of chest/abdomen every 6 months for 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing information  
- Detailed performance status (ECOG/ASA) and cardiopulmonary evaluation results.  
- Baseline liver function tests and volumetric FLR calculation.  
- Precise T and N staging of the primary tumor (CT or endoscopic ultrasound data).  
- Histologic grade and presence of lymphovascular or perineural invasion from biopsy.  
- BRAF mutation status (not provided) and any other molecular markers that could influence adjuvant therapy choice.  
- Confirmation of absence of extra‑hepatic disease with chest CT or PET‑CT.  
- Nutritional parameters (albumin, weight loss) to assess peri‑operative risk.

• Rationale:  
  – Two liver metastases, each ≤3 cm, located in separate, non‑adjacent segments (II and V).  
  – No radiologic evidence of major vascular or biliary invasion reported.  
  – No extra‑hepatic disease on thoraco‑abdominal CT.  
  – Primary tumor is symptomatic (obstruction) and can be addressed surgically; removal of segments II and V would leave a sufficient future liver remnant in a normal liver.  
  – RAS wild‑type status and low tumor burden meet current criteria for curative intent surgery.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Urgent primary tumor control – Perform a left‑sided colectomy (segmental resection or left hemicolectomy) to relieve obstruction. Rationale: symptomatic primary lesion is priority; resection eliminates source of complications and provides pathology for grading.  
B. Post‑operative recovery and systemic therapy – After adequate wound healing (≈2 weeks), initiate peri‑operative chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX ± anti‑VEGF). Rationale: standard of care for resectable synchronous liver metastases to treat micrometastatic disease and improve disease‑free survival.  
C. Curative liver resection – Plan a staged or simultaneous hepatic resection of segment II (left lateral segmentectomy) and segment V (segmentectomy or wedge resection). If intra‑operative assessment confirms adequate FLR and no unexpected vascular involvement, a simultaneous colon‑liver operation can be performed; otherwise, schedule liver surgery after completion of chemotherapy. Rationale: both lesions are amenable to anatomic or non‑anatomic resection with clear margins while preserving liver function.  
D. Adjuvant follow‑up – Continue surveillance with serial CEA, cross‑sectional imaging, and consider additional systemic therapy based on final pathology (grade, margins, nodal status). Rationale: to detect recurrence early and provide further systemic control if indicated.

Step 3 – Missing information  
• Histologic grade/differentiation of the primary colon cancer.  
• Detailed assessment of vascular (portal/hepatic artery) and biliary involvement of the liver lesions.  
• Liver‑specific imaging (gadolinium‑enhanced MRI or contrast‑enhanced ultrasound) to confirm lesion characteristics and plan resection.  
• Calculation of future liver remnant (FLR) volume or FLR % to ensure safety of hepatic resection.  
• Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, ICG clearance) and performance status (ECOG/ASA).  
• Whether any neoadjuvant/induction chemotherapy has already been given.  
• Exact surgical margins anticipated for the colon resection (T‑stage, nodal status).  

These data are needed to finalize the operative plan and confirm that simultaneous resection is safe for this patient.

   1. Complete colon resection first (as in A).

   – Rationale: ensures patient safety while still achieving curative intent.

   – Rationale: improves disease‑free survival and addresses occult micrometastatic disease.

- Presence of lymphovascular or perineural invasion in the primary.

- Any prior neoadjuvant therapy (none reported, but confirmation needed).  
- Patient’s preference regarding simultaneous versus staged surgery.  

These data are required to confirm that simultaneous resection is safe and to finalize peri‑operative planning.

Woman, 56 years old, incidental discovery of a right colon tumor during a workup for iron deficiency anemia. Thoraco-Abdominal CT scan shows an ileocecal mass and a single 2.5 cm metastasis in segment VI. CEA 35 ng/mL, KRAS mutation present. No other lesions on FDG-PET.
MDT Discussion: Single peripheral metastasis, situation suitable for combined surgical treatment.
Model_Alone:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (curative intent)  
- Rationale:  
  • Single hepatic lesion, 2.5 cm, peripheral (segment VI) – amenable to wedge resection or segmentectomy with adequate margins.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease on FDG‑PET; solitary extra‑hepatic site absent.  
  • Primary tumor confined to right colon (ileocecal region) without radiologic evidence of adjacent organ invasion.  
  • Expected future liver remnant >30 % after limited resection; no underlying liver disease reported.  
  • Patient age (56) and presumed adequate performance status support operative tolerance.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive pre‑operative work‑up  
   – Colonoscopy with biopsy confirmation, endoscopic tattooing of the tumor for intra‑operative localization.  
   – Baseline labs: liver function panel, coagulation profile, CEA trend, KRAS status already known.  
   – Cardiopulmonary assessment (e.g., ECG, echocardiogram, pulmonary function if indicated).  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (optional but preferred)  
   – 3–4 cycles of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) given the KRAS‑mutated, CEA‑elevated disease to address micrometastatic burden and assess tumor biology.  
   – Re‑staging CT/MRI after chemotherapy to confirm stability or response of the liver lesion and exclude new sites.  

C. Surgical resection (simultaneous approach)  
   – Right hemicolectomy with oncologic lymphadenectomy for the primary tumor.  
   – Anatomical segment VI resection (segmentectomy) or non‑anatomic wedge resection achieving ≥1 cm margin, performed during the same operation.  
   – Rationale: limited hepatic disease, peripheral location, and low operative morbidity allow a single‑stage procedure, reducing overall treatment time and hospitalizations.  

D. Post‑operative adjuvant therapy  
   – Completion of a total of 6 months peri‑operative chemotherapy (additional 2–3 cycles post‑op if neoadjuvant given).  
   – Surveillance plan: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing information  
- Exact performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities (cardiac, pulmonary, hepatic).  
- Detailed liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, INR, platelet count) and assessment of future liver remnant volume.  
- Pathologic stage of the primary tumor (T‑stage, nodal involvement) from colonoscopy/biopsy.  
- Presence or absence of synchronous lymph node metastasis on imaging or intra‑operative assessment.  
- Patient’s preference regarding neoadjuvant chemotherapy versus upfront surgery.  
- Any prior abdominal surgeries that might influence operative planning.

- No additional intra‑ or extra‑hepatic disease on FDG‑PET; therefore disease burden is limited to one hepatic site.  
- Future liver remnant will remain well above the 30 % functional threshold after a segmental resection of segment VI; portal vein embolization is unnecessary.  
- No reported contraindicating comorbidities or impaired liver function.  
- Although the metastasis is synchronous, the small size and solitary nature outweigh the negative predictive impact of synchrony and KRAS mutation.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Pre‑operative work‑up (within 2 weeks)  
   • High‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to confirm lesion size, location and exclude occult disease.  
   • Full laboratory panel (LFTs, bilirubin, INR, albumin, renal function) and assessment of performance status (ECOG/ASA).  
   • Multidisciplinary confirmation of fitness for combined surgery.  
   Rationale: ensures accurate anatomic mapping and verifies that the patient can tolerate a simultaneous procedure.  

B. Short‑course neoadjuvant systemic therapy (2–3 cycles, 6–8 weeks)  
   • Regimen: FOLFOX (or CAPEOX) ± bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF), given KRAS‑mutated status precludes anti‑EGFR agents.  
   Rationale: in synchronous disease with elevated CEA (35 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation, a brief chemotherapy window tests tumor biology, may further downsize the metastasis, and provides early systemic control.  

C. Simultaneous curative‑intent surgery (within 4–6 weeks after chemotherapy)  
   • Right hemicolectomy with oncologic lymphadenectomy (D3) for the ileocecal primary.  
   • Anatomical segment VI resection (segmentectomy or wedge) aiming for ≥1 cm macroscopic margin (R0).  
   • Intra‑operative ultrasound to reconfirm absence of additional lesions.  
   Rationale: the hepatic lesion is peripheral and small, allowing a limited liver resection that can be safely combined with the colorectal operation, reducing total hospital stay and avoiding two separate recovery periods.  

D. Adjuvant systemic therapy and surveillance  
   • Complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy (additional 3–4 cycles post‑op).  
   • Follow‑up: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest/abdomen every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  
   Rationale: consolidates systemic disease control, addresses micrometastatic risk, and enables early detection of recurrence.  

Step 3 – Missing information  
- Detailed performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidity profile (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Baseline liver function tests and volumetric assessment of future liver remnant.  
- Pathologic staging of the primary tumor (T stage, nodal status N) from colonoscopy biopsy or imaging.  
- Exact histologic grade and presence of lymph‑vascular or perineural invasion in the primary.  
- Confirmation of negative chest imaging (CT rather than PET alone) to rule out pulmonary metastases.  
- Patient’s preferences regarding timing of surgery versus chemotherapy.  

These data are needed to finalize peri‑operative risk assessment and to tailor the chemotherapy regimen precisely.

Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline resectable but likely resectable after confirmation of hepatic functional reserve).  
- Justification:  
  • Single liver lesion, 2.5 cm, located peripherally in segment VI – meets size and number criteria for hepatic resection.  
  • No radiologic evidence of major vascular (portal or hepatic vein) invasion or biliary involvement reported.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease identified on thoraco‑abdominal CT and FDG‑PET.  
  • Assuming adequate future liver remnant (FLR) – typical for a solitary peripheral lesion in the right liver.  
  • Primary colorectal tumor still present; resection of the colon primary is required before or in conjunction with liver surgery, influencing timing but not the intrinsic resectability of the metastasis.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   – Obtain high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to confirm lesion characteristics, vascular anatomy, and FLR volume.  
   – Perform colonoscopy with biopsy to grade differentiation and assess obstruction/perforation risk.  
   – Baseline labs (CEA trend, liver function, carcino‑embryonic antigen, KRAS confirmed).  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (6 cycles)  
   – Regimen: FOLFOX (or CAPOX) combined with bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF) given KRAS mutation precludes anti‑EGFR agents.  
   – Rationale: Assess tumor biology, potential down‑staging, and treat micrometastatic disease; also allows time to complete staging work‑up and optimize patient’s nutritional/functional status.  

C. Surgical resection (performed after restaging post‑chemotherapy)  
   – Option 1 (preferred if patient is fit): Simultaneous resection – right hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis plus anatomical segment VI resection (segmentectomy or wedge) in the same operation.  
   – Option 2 (if concern for operative time or liver quality): Staged approach – first right hemicolectomy, recover 4–6 weeks, then liver resection.  
   – Rationale: Single peripheral metastasis allows limited hepatic resection with low morbidity; simultaneous surgery reduces total hospital stay and avoids delay in oncologic control.  

D. Adjuvant therapy  
   – Resume or complete a total of 12 cycles of systemic chemotherapy (including the neoadjuvant cycles) post‑operatively, adjusting based on pathologic response and tolerance.  
   – Consider enrollment in clinical trial or use of maintenance bevacizumab if indicated.  

Step 3 – Missing information  
- Histologic grade of differentiation of the primary tumor.  
- Confirmation whether the colorectal primary has already been resected.  
- Presence or absence of obstructive, perforative, or active bleeding symptoms from the primary lesion.  
- Detailed hepatic vascular anatomy and any contact/invasion of portal/hepatic veins.  
- Results of liver MRI (including FLR volumetry).  
- Baseline and post‑chemotherapy FLR ratio to ensure safe hepatic resection.  
- Status of any prior systemic chemotherapy (has any been given already?).  
- Assessment of arterial anatomy (e.g., variant hepatic arterial supply).  
- Patient’s performance status, comorbidities, and liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin).  
- Planned surgical margins (R0 feasibility) based on intra‑operative ultrasound.  

These data are essential to finalize resectability, choose between simultaneous versus staged surgery, and tailor peri‑operative management.

Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- The patient has a single peripheral liver metastasis measuring 2.5 cm in segment VI, no vascular or biliary invasion reported, and no extra‑hepatic disease on PET‑CT.  
- Current oncologic criteria define resectability as the ability to achieve an R0 resection of all disease while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow, outflow and a future liver remnant (FLR) >30 % in normal liver.  
- Resection of a solitary sub‑segmental lesion in segment VI would leave the majority of the liver intact; the expected FLR is well above the safety threshold.  
- Therefore, the disease is resectable (not merely potentially resectable) according to standard hepatobiliary oncology guidelines.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive pre‑operative work‑up  
   - Obtain a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or gadoxetate‑enhanced MRI) to confirm lesion size, exact location, relationship to hepatic vessels, and to exclude occult lesions.  
   - Perform colonoscopy with biopsy if not already done, and stage the primary tumor (T/N status, differentiation).  
   - Assess patient fitness (ECOG/ASA, cardiopulmonary reserve, liver function tests) and calculate FLR volume (CT‑based volumetry).  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (optional but recommended)  
   - Because the metastasis is technically resectable but the primary tumor is still in situ, give 3–4 cycles of a fluoropyrimidine‑oxaliplatin doublet (e.g., mFOLFOX6) plus a VEGF‑targeted agent (bevacizumab) – anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective with KRAS mutation.  
   - Rationale: peri‑operative chemotherapy improves disease‑free survival, allows assessment of tumor biology, and may down‑size the lesion further, facilitating a margin‑negative liver resection.  

C. Surgical phase – Simultaneous (combined) resection  
   - Perform a right hemicolectomy (ileocecal resection with adequate lymphadenectomy) together with a segment VI wedge/segmentectomy or non‑anatomical resection of the metastasis.  
   - Rationale: the primary tumor is asymptomatic, the liver lesion is peripheral and small, and combined surgery avoids a second operation, shortens overall treatment time, and is supported by the MDT’s statement that the situation is suitable for combined surgical treatment.  

D. Post‑operative management  
   - Resume systemic chemotherapy (completion of 6 months total, including pre‑operative cycles) with the same regimen used pre‑operatively, adjusted for postoperative recovery.  
   - Monitor CEA and perform surveillance imaging (CT or MRI of liver, chest CT) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  
   - Provide standard postoperative care (DVT prophylaxis, early mobilization, nutritional support) and assess for any complications (Clavien‑Dindo grading).  

Step 3 – Missing information  
- Primary tumor pathology: grade of differentiation, T‑stage, N‑stage, presence of lymphovascular or perineural invasion.  
- Confirmation whether the primary colorectal tumor has already been resected or is still in situ.  
- Clinical symptomatology of the primary (obstruction, perforation, active bleeding).  
- Detailed hepatic vascular anatomy and any microscopic vascular contact or invasion of the metastasis.  
- Results of a liver‑specific MRI (or at least confirmation that no additional occult lesions exist).  
- Planned or already administered systemic chemotherapy regimen and number of cycles given.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volumetric data and calculated FLR ratio.  
- Patient performance status (ECOG/ASA), comorbidities, and baseline liver function tests.  
- Planned margin goal (target >1 cm or R0) and intra‑operative ultrasound findings.  

These data are needed to finalize peri‑operative planning and to confirm that the simultaneous resection can be safely undertaken.

Man, 68 years old, history of smoking, presenting with T3N1 upper rectal adenocarcinoma with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis in segment III. Pelvic MRI: limited parietal invasion. CEA 45 ng/mL. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Single resectable metastasis, possibility of coordinated surgical treatment after short-course radiotherapy.
Model_Alone:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline between clearly resectable and requiring optimization).  
- Rationale:  
   Liver lesion: solitary 1.8 cm metastasis in segment III, amenable to limited anatomic or non‑anatomic resection with preservation of a sufficient future liver remnant (>30 % in a normal liver).  
   Primary tumor: T3N1 upper rectal adenocarcinoma with limited parietal invasion; no circumferential resection margin (CRM) involvement on MRI, making sphincter‑preserving resection feasible.  
   No documented extra‑hepatic disease; CEA elevated but not a contraindication.  
   Patient age 68, smoking history only; assuming adequate performance status and liver function, combined or staged resection is technically possible.  

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Short‑course radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) to the rectum – to achieve local tumor down‑staging while minimizing treatment delay for the liver lesion.  
B. Neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 3–4 cycles FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR antibody given RAS wild‑type) – to treat micrometastatic disease, assess tumor biology, and potentially further shrink the liver metastasis if needed.  
C. Surgical resection (simultaneous approach) – perform low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision together with a wedge/segmental resection of segment III. Rationale: small peripheral liver lesion allows safe concurrent resection, reduces overall treatment time, and avoids two separate major operations.  
D. Adjuvant systemic therapy (completion of peri‑operative chemotherapy to a total of 6–8 cycles) – to consolidate response and address any residual microscopic disease.  

Step 3 - Missing information  
- Current performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Baseline liver function tests and volumetric assessment of future liver remnant.  
- Detailed MRI report on mesorectal fascia involvement and distance of tumor from the anal verge.  
- Chest imaging (CT) to confirm absence of pulmonary metastases.  
- Full molecular profile (BRAF, MSI status) that could influence systemic therapy choice.  
- CEA trend over time and any prior response to therapy.  
- Patient preference regarding sphincter preservation versus abdominoperineal resection.  
- Details of smoking history (pack‑years) and any ongoing use that may affect peri‑operative risk.

Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Resectable  
- Rationale:  
  • Single hepatic lesion, 1.8 cm, located in segment III – amenable to wedge resection or limited segmentectomy with preservation of ≥2 contiguous liver segments and an adequate future liver remnant (>30 % in a normal liver).  
  • No radiologically evident extra‑hepatic disease (chest CT/MRI not reported but presumed negative by MDT).  
  • Primary rectal tumor is T3N1, limited parietal invasion, technically resectable by low anterior resection (LAR).  
  • RAS wild‑type, CEA moderately elevated but not prohibitive.  
  • Patient’s age (68) and smoking history do not preclude surgery provided functional status is acceptable.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Short‑course pre‑operative radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) to the rectum.  
   – Rationale: Provides local control of the T3 rectal lesion, creates a treatment window for hepatic surgery, and is standard for upper rectal cancers when long‑course chemoradiation is not required.  

B. Peri‑operative systemic chemotherapy (4–6 cycles of FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody, e.g., cetuximab, given RAS wild‑type).  
   – Rationale: Treats micrometastatic disease, serves as a biological test of tumor aggressiveness, and may further down‑size the liver lesion if needed.  

C. Restaging imaging (contrast‑enhanced liver MRI or multiphase CT, plus chest CT) after chemotherapy.  
   – Rationale: Confirms that the hepatic metastasis remains resectable, excludes new extra‑hepatic sites, and assesses FLR volume.  

D. Coordinated surgical resection – preferred simultaneous minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic LAR + laparoscopic segment III wedge resection) performed 4–6 weeks after radiotherapy, provided the patient’s operative risk is low.  
   – Rationale: Both procedures are limited in extent; simultaneous resection avoids a second hospitalization, shortens overall treatment time, and is supported by literature for minor hepatectomy combined with low anterior resection when the primary is asymptomatic after radiotherapy.  

   If intra‑operative assessment reveals inadequate FLR or unexpected disease, convert to a staged approach (liver‑first then rectal resection 4–6 weeks later).  

Step 3 – Missing information  
- Detailed performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and cardiopulmonary reserve (e.g., VO₂ max, cardiac evaluation).  
- Baseline liver function tests and calculation of future liver remnant volume.  
- Full thoracic imaging to definitively rule out pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic metastases.  
- Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge and mesorectal fascia involvement on MRI (to confirm feasibility of sphincter‑preserving LAR).  
- Comorbidities beyond smoking (e.g., diabetes, cardiovascular disease, renal function).  
- Patient preference regarding timing of surgeries and willingness for minimally invasive techniques.  
- Nutritional status and serum albumin level.  

These data are needed to finalize operative risk assessment and confirm that the proposed simultaneous strategy is safe for this individual.

A. Comprehensive restaging  
   – Obtain contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT and liver MRI with liver‑specific contrast.  
   – Rationale: Confirm absence of extra‑hepatic metastases, delineate hepatic vasculature, assess FLR, and verify that the lesion has no major vascular or biliary invasion.

   – Deliver short‑course radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) followed by a 4‑week interval.  
   – Consider adding systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 4 cycles of FOLFOX) during the interval because of synchronous liver disease and N‑positive status.

   - Rationale: T2N0 rectal tumors, especially those located in the mid‑ or low‑rectum, benefit from pre‑operative CRT to improve local control and down‑stage the tumor, facilitating sphincter‑preserving surgery.

   - Timing: 4–6 weeks after rectal surgery, provided the patient has recovered and liver function is adequate.

   - Rationale: Isolated, small lesion permits curative‑intent resection; staged approach reduces operative stress and allows optimal postoperative monitoring.

   - Rationale: Depending on final pathology (e.g., lymphovascular invasion, margin status), additional cycles of oxaliplatin‑based chemotherapy may be offered to reduce recurrence risk.

Man, 64 years old, history of rectal resection (T3N1) 2 years ago. Liver MRI: two liver metastases, segments II and VIII, 2.5 and 3 cm. Thoracic CT scan negative for metastases. KRAS mutated, CEA 240 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metachronous recurrence, technically accessible.

Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Two isolated metastases, each ≤3 cm, located in segments II (left lateral) and VIII (right posterior) – within the size and number limits for hepatic resection.  
  • No radiologic evidence of extra‑hepatic disease (negative thoracic CT).  
  • Bilobar distribution is technically feasible with a parenchymal‑sparing approach; anticipated future liver remnant >30 % in a patient with normal liver.  
  • Prior rectal resection does not preclude hepatic surgery; no reported hepatic dysfunction or portal hypertension.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic peri‑operative chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles FOLFOX ± bevacizumab)  
   – Rationale: KRAS mutation and markedly elevated CEA suggest aggressive tumor biology; peri‑operative chemotherapy improves disease‑free survival and provides a test of tumor responsiveness.  

B. Restaging with contrast‑enhanced MRI and CT after chemotherapy  
   – Rationale: Confirm disease stability or response, reassess resectability, and evaluate FLR volume.  

C. Parenchymal‑sparing liver resection (segmentectomy or wedge resection of segment II and segment VIII lesions)  
   – Rationale: Achieve R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver tissue; both lesions are amenable to non‑anatomic or limited anatomic resections without need for portal vein embolization.  

D. Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (completion of planned 12‑cycle regimen)  
   – Rationale: Consolidate systemic control, given high pre‑operative CEA and KRAS‑mutated disease.  

Step 3 – Missing information  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, AST/ALT, INR, platelets) and volumetric assessment of future liver remnant.  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities that could affect tolerance of chemotherapy or surgery.  
- Details of any prior adjuvant therapy after the initial rectal resection (type, duration, response).  
- Exact relationship of the hepatic lesions to major vascular structures (proximity to hepatic veins, portal pedicles) to confirm feasibility of a parenchymal‑sparing approach.  
- Current status of the rectal anastomosis (symptoms, surveillance findings) to ensure no occult local recurrence.

Woman, 58 years old, left T4aN2M1 colon cancer with multiple bilobar metastases. After 6 cycles FOLFOX + bevacizumab: 60% volumetric reduction, CEA dropped from 880 to 180 ng/mL. Liver MRI: 5 remaining lesions, well-defined.
MDT Discussion: Major response to chemotherapy, surgical conversion considered.
Model_Alone:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Five residual hepatic lesions are well‑defined after a 60 % volumetric response, indicating a favorable tumor biology and chemosensitivity.  
  • CEA decline from 880 to 180 ng/mL supports biochemical response.  
  • Bilobar distribution remains, which traditionally limits immediate one‑stage resection unless an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved.  
  • No information is provided regarding lesion size, proximity to major hepatic vessels/ducts, or FLR volume; therefore, definitive resectability cannot be confirmed, but conversion to resectability is plausible with appropriate adjuncts (e.g., portal vein embolization, two‑stage or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy – ALPPS).  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging (within 2–3 weeks).  
   - Perform contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary phase and CT chest/abdomen/pelvis to define lesion size, segmental location, vascular involvement, and to rule out extra‑hepatic disease.  
   - Obtain liver function tests, indocyanine‑green clearance or 99mTc‑mebrofenin hepatobiliary scintigraphy, and calculate FLR volume using volumetric software.  

B. Multidisciplinary decision on surgical approach (after restaging).  
   - If FLR ≥30 % in a normal liver (or ≥40 % in a chemotherapy‑injured liver) and lesions are amenable to R0 resection, plan a single‑stage combined colorectal and hepatic resection (simultaneous) or a staged approach (colon first, then liver) based on patient performance status and operative risk.  
   - If FLR is insufficient, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) or ALPPS to hypertrophy the future remnant, followed by delayed hepatic resection.  

C. Surgical execution.  
   - Perform oncologic resection of the primary left‑sided colon cancer with adequate lymphadenectomy (aim for ≥12 nodes).  
   - Conduct parenchymal‑sparing hepatic resections (segmentectomy/partial hepatectomy) to achieve negative margins while preserving maximal functional liver tissue.  
   - Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion boundaries and guide resection.  

D. Adjuvant systemic therapy.  
   - Resume or modify systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) for 3–6 months post‑operatively, considering the prior bevacizumab exposure and any molecular markers (RAS/RAF status).  
   - Monitor CEA and imaging every 3–4 months for surveillance.  

Step 3 – Missing information  
- Exact size and segmental location of each hepatic lesion.  
- Distance of lesions to major hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and biliary structures.  
- Quantitative FLR volume and baseline liver function (bilirubin, albumin, ICG clearance, etc.).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky), comorbidities, and cardiopulmonary reserve.  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI status).  
- Current status of the primary tumor (symptomatic obstruction, perforation, or bleeding).  
- Details of prior chemotherapy tolerance and cumulative oxaliplatin exposure (risk of sinusoidal injury).  

These data are essential to finalize resectability, select the optimal surgical sequence, and tailor peri‑operative management.

   – Resume systemic chemotherapy (or switch to maintenance) after recovery, tailored to molecular profile once available.  
   – Rationale: Reduces risk of recurrence in the setting of high baseline CEA and multiple initial lesions.

- Patient‑related factors: comorbidities, prior abdominal surgeries, and willingness for major hepatic resection.

  • The lesions have progressed after 8 cycles of FOLFOX, indicating chemoresistance and aggressive disease.  
  • Rising CEA (950 ng/mL) supports biologically aggressive disease.  
  • Current MDT consensus states “no surgical window,” reflecting that the disease is not presently amenable to curative resection.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Second‑line systemic therapy – initiate FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab (or enrol in a clinical trial).  
   – Rationale: aim to achieve disease control or down‑staging when first‑line FOLFOX failed.  

B. Re‑evaluation after 2–3 months – repeat contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI, assess CEA trend, and evaluate performance status.  
   – Rationale: determine whether the tumor has stabilized, responded, or further progressed.  

C. Conversion to resectability (if imaging shows response or stable disease) – plan right hepatectomy (or parenchymal‑sparing resection) ensuring ≥30 % future liver remnant and negative margins.  
   – Rationale: conversion surgery is feasible only after achieving at least disease stability; adequate FLR must be confirmed.  

D. Palliative/locoregional options (if disease continues to progress) – consider Y‑90 radio‑embolization, percutaneous ablation, or best‑supportive care.  
   – Rationale: provides symptom control and may modestly prolong survival when curative intent is no longer possible.  

Step 3 – Missing information  
- Current Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status / comorbidity profile.  
- Baseline and current liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count).  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume assessment.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
- Status of the primary colon tumor (resected, symptomatic, obstructive).  
- Molecular profile beyond KRAS (BRAF, MSI‑high status).  
- Detailed trend of CEA over time (baseline, peak, response).  
- Prior toxicity or tolerance to FOLFOX.  

Without these data a definitive surgical plan cannot be finalized.

Woman, 62 years old, left colon adenocarcinoma with seven liver metastases. After 6 cycles FOLFOX + panitumumab: complete disappearance of four foci and reduction of others at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA normalized.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response in several segments, uncertainty regarding microscopic persistence.

Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Rationale:  
  • Seven hepatic metastases initially, but after 6 cycles of FOLFOX + panitumumab four lesions are radiologically absent and the remaining lesions have decreased in size, indicating good tumor response.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease; CEA normalization supports systemic disease control.  
  • Resectability hinges on ability to achieve an R0 resection with an adequate future liver remnant (FLR). Because the exact distribution and residual tumor burden are not detailed, the case cannot be declared outright resectable, but the response makes a curative‑intent liver operation feasible pending further anatomic assessment.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Restaging imaging – Obtain a high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast (gadoxetate) and a PET‑CT.  
   • Purpose: confirm the true extent of residual disease, detect any occult extra‑hepatic sites, and allow precise volumetric calculation of the FLR.  

B. Multidisciplinary re‑evaluation – Review imaging, liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ICG clearance), and performance status.  
   • If lesions are confined to one lobe or can be cleared with a single‑stage resection leaving an FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % in steatotic or chemotherapy‑injured liver), proceed to curative surgery.  
   • If disease is bilobar with insufficient FLR, consider a staged approach (e.g., portal vein embolization to hypertrophy the future remnant, two‑stage hepatectomy, or ALPPS) based on lesion location.  

C. Surgical resection – Perform liver‑directed surgery with intra‑operative ultrasound to locate any residual foci.  
   • Aim for R0 margins; use parenchymal‑sparing techniques when possible to preserve liver volume.  
   • If complete radiologic response is confirmed in some segments, those areas may be resected or left in situ after intra‑operative confirmation of negative margins.  

D. Adjuvant systemic therapy and surveillance – Resume systemic therapy (continue anti‑EGFR if still indicated, or switch to a fluoropyrimidine‑based regimen) for 3–6 months post‑operatively, followed by serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for the first two years.  

Step 3 – Missing information  
- Precise anatomic location (segmental distribution) and current size of the residual liver lesions.  
- Volumetric data: calculated future liver remnant volume and baseline liver volume.  
- Liver functional reserve: Child‑Pugh score, ICG‑R15, presence of steatosis or chemotherapy‑associated liver injury.  
- Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities that may affect surgical risk.  
- Confirmation of absence of extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., lung nodules, peritoneal implants) on PET‑CT or dedicated imaging.  
- Molecular profile beyond EGFR‑targeted therapy eligibility (e.g., BRAF status) that could influence adjuvant choices.

   - Rationale: Consolidate response and treat potential micrometastatic disease; regimen may be continued FOLFOXIRI or switched to a maintenance protocol (e.g., fluoropyrimidine ± bevacizumab) based on tolerance and molecular profile.

   - Initiate 6–8 cycles of FOLFOXIRI ± anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS wild‑type, aiming for maximal tumor shrinkage in liver and lung and early treatment of micrometastatic disease.
